svg.aria-label: Diagram: Azure virtual networks and subnets, the five reserved addresses, size bounds and scoping. Azure reserves the first four addresses and the last address, for a total of five IP addresses within each subnet. For 192.168.1.0/24 these are 192.168.1.0 as the network address, 192.168.1.1 reserved for the default gateway, 192.168.1.2 and 192.168.1.3 reserved to map the Azure DNS IP addresses into the virtual network space, and 192.168.1.255 as the network broadcast address. Consequently a slash 29, the smallest supported subnet, yields three usable addresses out of eight; a slash 28 yields eleven of sixteen; a slash 27 yields twenty-seven of thirty-two; a slash 24 yields two hundred fifty-one of two hundred fifty-six. Microsoft's own example confirms it: a VM deployed into 10.0.0.0/16 receives a private IP similar to 10.0.0.4, the fifth address. Size bounds are that the smallest supported IPv4 subnet is slash 29 and the largest is slash 2, while IPv6 subnets must be exactly slash 64. Five address ranges cannot be added to a virtual network at all: 224.0.0.0/4 for multicast, 255.255.255.255/32 for broadcast, 127.0.0.0/8 for loopback, 169.254.0.0/16 for link local, and 168.63.129.16/32 for internal DNS. Recommended ranges are those in RFC 1918, and the shared address space of RFC 6598 can also be deployed. Virtual networks are Layer 3 overlays and Azure does not support any Layer 2 semantics, so VLANs cannot be brought to Azure. A virtual network is scoped to a single region and to a single subscription; virtual networks in different regions connect through Virtual Network Peering. Subnet address spaces cannot overlap one another, and a virtual network can link to other virtual networks and to on-premises networks only as long as the CIDR blocks do not overlap. Public IP addresses can exist in a virtual network but are not directly accessible from the internet, a private IP cannot be reserved for a virtual machine created later, and UDP ports 4791 and 65330 are reserved for the host. Microsoft's planning guidance is that subnets should not cover the entire address space of the virtual network, that a few large virtual networks are preferable to many small ones within a subscription, and simultaneously that the landing zone principle of subscription democratization favours many subscriptions each with their own virtual network, commonly implemented as hub and spoke or Virtual WAN.
svg.title: Five addresses gone from every subnet, and the arithmetic decides the topology
svg.text: “Azure reserves the first four addresses and the last address, for a total of five IP addresses”
… within each subnet. A traditional network reserves two. That difference decides more designs than any diagram.
Where the five go, for 192.168.1.0/24
“Network address” — familiar
“Reserved by Azure for the default gateway”
“Reserved by Azure to map the Azure DNS IP addresses to the
virtual network space” — the two nobody budgets for
“Network broadcast address” — familiar
Microsoft’s own example confirms it: deploy a VM into 10.0.0.0/16 and “a private IP similar to 10.0.0.4 is assigned”.
Not .1. The first address a workload ever gets is the fifth one.
So size subnets by usable count, not by mask
SUBNET
TOTAL
RESERVED
USABLE
WASTED
/29 (the floor)
/27 (practical floor)
Hard bounds
“The smallest supported IPv4 subnet is /29, and the largest
is /2 (using CIDR subnet definitions).”
“IPv6 subnets must be exactly /64 in size.”
So IPv6 planning is only ever how MANY, never how big.
No /30 or /31 point-to-point links the way physical kit does.
Recommended: RFC 1918 — and RFC 6598 shared space is
Five ranges you cannot add at all
224.0.0.0/4 — multicast
127.0.0.0/8 — loopback
168.63.129.16/32 — internal DNS (Azure-specific)
That last one is worth knowing by sight: it turns up in NSG
rules and health-probe sources across the platform.
The eight words that invalidate a category of on-premises design
“Virtual networks are Layer 3 overlays. Azure does not support any Layer 2 semantics.” Can you bring your VLANs? “No.”
No VLAN trunking, no broadcast discovery, no gratuitous ARP for failover, no virtual MAC sharing. A cluster that fails over
by moving a MAC address needs a different mechanism here — better found on this page than during a cutover.
Two scoping rules, and one constraint that governs everything
Region
“scoped to a single region/location” — multi-region means peering, never a stretched VNet
Subscription
“scoped to a subscription” — the same boundary post #60 found for identity
Overlap
subnets can’t overlap; linking VNets or on-premises works only if CIDR blocks don’t
Microsoft’s two planning rules read as a contradiction and are not: “a few large virtual networks instead of multiple small
ones” is scoped WITHIN a subscription, while Subscription Democratization wants many subscriptions each with their own.
Resolution: many subscriptions, few VNets in each, hub and spoke. And “subnets shouldn’t cover the entire address space”
— the cheapest advice on the page, and the one that cannot be retrofitted once you need an unplanned subnet.
Sources: Azure Virtual Network FAQ, and Azure Virtual Network concepts and best practices, on Microsoft Learn.
